title: The Three Suitors
summary: A beautiful woman dies and three suitors each use their powers to revive her. Betal asks Vikram — who deserves to marry her?
moral: True love is selfless sacrifice

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal tells the tale of three men who each loved the same woman

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram considers each suitor's claim — one preserved her ashes, one found the mantra, one recited it

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram rules that the one who recited the mantra is like a father, the ash-keeper like a son, and only the finder is the true husband

title: The Transposed Heads
summary: Two friends' heads are accidentally swapped onto each other's bodies. Betal asks — which resulting man is the woman's husband?
moral: Identity lies in the mind, not the body

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal narrates how two friends sacrificed themselves at a temple and were revived with swapped heads

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram weighs whether the husband is defined by his head or his body

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram declares the man with the husband's head is the true husband, for the head governs the person

title: The Father and Son Who Married Mother and Daughter
summary: A father marries the daughter and his son marries the mother. What is the relationship between their children?
moral: Relationships must be examined beyond surface appearances

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal describes the unusual cross-generational marriages

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram untangles the complex family relationships

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram explains the paradoxical kinship — each child is simultaneously uncle and nephew to the other

title: The King Who Sacrificed His Son
summary: A king must sacrifice his own son to save his kingdom from a demon. Was the king right to do so?
moral: A ruler's duty to his people can demand the ultimate sacrifice

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal tells of a king whose kingdom was cursed unless he offered his son's blood

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram weighs a father's love against a king's duty

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram judges the king was righteous — dharma demanded he place his kingdom above personal grief

title: The Faithful Wife
summary: A devoted wife follows her dead husband's spirit, braving demons and darkness. Betal asks if her devotion was wisdom or folly.
moral: True devotion transcends even death

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal narrates how the wife entered the cremation ground to retrieve her husband's soul

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram considers whether such extreme devotion is virtuous or reckless

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram praises her courage — love that conquers fear of death is the highest virtue

title: The Merchant's Generous Son
summary: A merchant's son gives away everything he owns, even his own flesh, to help others. Is he noble or a fool?
moral: Generosity without wisdom leads to ruin

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal describes a young man who gave his wealth, his house, and finally his own body to those in need

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram considers the line between selfless charity and self-destruction

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram declares that charity must be measured — giving that destroys the giver helps no one in the end

title: The Brave Princess Who Chose Death
summary: A princess chooses to die rather than marry a wicked king. Betal asks if she was brave or wasteful of life.
moral: Honor and freedom are worth more than a life of subjugation

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal tells of a princess captured by a tyrant who chose poison over marriage

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram weighs whether preserving life or preserving honor matters more

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram honors her choice — a life without dignity is no life at all

title: The Four Gifted Brothers
summary: Four brothers with supernatural skills — bone-reader, assembler, flesh-giver, life-giver — resurrect a lion that kills them. Who is to blame?
moral: Knowledge without wisdom is dangerous

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal tells how four learned brothers each used their gift on a pile of bones, creating a lion

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram considers which brother bears the most guilt for the deadly outcome

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram blames the life-giver — he had the final chance to stop and should have used judgment

title: The Hermit's Daughter
summary: A hermit transforms his daughter into different forms to test three suitors. Who truly loved her?
moral: True love sees beyond external beauty

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal describes how the hermit turned his daughter ugly, old, and then invisible

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram evaluates which suitor loved the woman herself versus her form

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram chooses the one who searched for her even when invisible — he loved her soul

title: The Thief Who Became a King
summary: A skilled thief steals for the poor and eventually saves the kingdom. Should he be punished or rewarded?
moral: Actions must be judged by their intent and outcome

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal narrates how a notorious thief robbed the corrupt rich to feed starving villages

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram weighs justice against compassion — theft is wrong, but the cause was noble

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram rules that intent matters — the thief's dharma was higher than the law he broke

title: The Parrot and the Maina
summary: A parrot and a maina bird debate whether men or women are more virtuous. Each tells stories to prove their point.
moral: Virtue knows no gender — it lives in individual hearts

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal presents the debate between the two birds before King Vikram

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram hears tales of virtuous men and women from each bird

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram declares that virtue belongs to individuals, not to any group

title: The Prince Who Married a Demoness
summary: A prince unknowingly marries a rakshasi who eats humans at night. When he discovers the truth, what should he do?
moral: Appearances can deceive; vigilance protects the innocent

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal tells how the prince discovered his beautiful wife feasting in the cremation ground

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram considers duty to a spouse versus duty to protect the people she devours

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram declares the prince must stop her — protecting the innocent outweighs marital loyalty to evil

title: The Brahmin and the Three Boons
summary: A brahmin receives three boons from a god but wastes them through poor choices. Who is truly at fault?
moral: Hasty wishes bring lasting regret

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal describes how the brahmin wasted each boon — one on greed, one on anger, one undoing the first two

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram considers whether the god was cruel to grant boons to a fool, or the man was simply unworthy

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram blames the brahmin — wisdom must precede power, or power destroys itself

title: The Soldier and the Sanyasi
summary: A soldier protects a sanyasi who later refuses to bless him, saying violence taints the soul. Who lived more righteously?
moral: Righteous action in the world is equal to righteous renunciation

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal tells how a soldier fought off bandits to save a meditating sanyasi

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram weighs the sanyasi's purity of non-violence against the soldier's protective violence

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram sides with the soldier — dharma performed in action is no less than dharma in meditation

title: The Ungrateful Goldsmith
summary: A man saves a goldsmith, a snake, a tiger, and a monkey from a well. The animals repay him but the goldsmith betrays him.
moral: Beasts may show more gratitude than humans

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal describes how each rescued creature responded — the animals with gifts, the goldsmith with treachery

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram reflects on human nature versus animal instinct

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram declares that gratitude is a measure of character, and the goldsmith proved himself lower than beasts

title: The Two Princes and the Enchanted Pool
summary: Two princes drink from a pool — one becomes a woman. They must decide who rules the kingdom now.
moral: True kingship is earned by wisdom, not by form

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal tells of the enchanted pool that transformed the elder prince

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram considers whether the transformed prince retains the right to rule

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram declares that the crown belongs to the wiser ruler regardless of form

title: The Devoted Servant
summary: A servant turns himself to stone to save his master from a prophecy. Was the master worthy of such sacrifice?
moral: Loyalty must be earned, not demanded

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal narrates how the servant overheard a deadly prophecy and sacrificed himself to prevent it

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram questions whether the master ever showed equal care for the servant

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram says the servant's nobility shames the master — true loyalty flows both ways

title: The Gambler's Wife
summary: A gambler loses everything including his wife in a bet. She wins herself back through her own cleverness.
moral: A person's freedom can never rightfully be wagered by another

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal tells how the wife was staked and lost, then challenged the winner to a contest of wits

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram considers the ethics of wagering another person's liberty

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram rules that no person can be another's property — the bet was void from the start

title: The Painted Bride
summary: An artist paints a portrait so beautiful that a king falls in love with it. But the real woman looks nothing like the painting.
moral: Love born from illusion cannot survive reality

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal tells how the king married the woman sight unseen based on the portrait

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram considers who is at fault — the king for his shallow love or the artist for his flattering brush

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram blames the king — he fell in love with paint, not a person

title: The Yogi and the King's Daughter
summary: A yogi uses magic to possess a dead king's body to marry a princess. Is this love or deception?
moral: Love obtained through deception is built on sand

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal tells how the yogi abandoned his body and entered the king's corpse to win the princess

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram weighs whether the yogi's devotion justifies the means

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram condemns the yogi — love requires truth, and the princess married a lie

title: The Three Sensitive Queens
summary: Three queens each claim supreme sensitivity — one bruised by a flower petal, one burned by moonlight, one hurt by the sound of a pestle. Who is most delicate?
moral: Excessive delicacy is a weakness disguised as refinement

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal describes the three queens' extraordinary sensitivities

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram ranks the claims, questioning which sensitivity is genuine

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram declares all three equally absurd — true strength is in resilience, not fragility

title: The Mendicant and the Jewel
summary: A mendicant finds a priceless jewel and must choose between keeping it and remaining pure. What does renunciation truly mean?
moral: True renunciation is freedom from attachment, not avoidance of objects

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal tells how the mendicant found the jewel and agonized over it for days

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram considers whether touching wealth taints a holy man

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram says true renunciation means the jewel has no power over him — he can give it away without a thought

title: The Clever Thief and the Brahmin
summary: A thief tricks a brahmin out of his sacrificial goat through three separate deceptions. Who is the bigger fool?
moral: A man who doubts his own eyes is easily robbed

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal tells how three men each told the brahmin his goat was actually a dog

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram weighs whether the brahmin's trust was naive or the thieves' trick was brilliant

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram faults the brahmin — he abandoned his own senses for the word of strangers

title: The Girl Who Was Revived Twice
summary: A girl dies twice and is revived by two different men. Each claims to be her destined partner.
moral: Destiny is not ownership — saving a life does not buy a soul

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal describes the two revivals — once by a physician, once by a yogi

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram considers whether saving a life creates an obligation of love

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram says neither man owns her — the girl must choose for herself

title: The Final Riddle — Vikram's Silence
summary: Betal poses a riddle so perfectly balanced that no answer can be given. Vikram finally stays silent, and Betal is captured at last.
moral: Sometimes the wisest answer is silence

acts.name: riddle
acts.summary: Betal poses his final impossible dilemma to Vikram

acts.name: debate
acts.summary: Vikram recognizes that any answer will be wrong — the trap is in answering

acts.name: answer
acts.summary: Vikram stays silent; Betal, unable to return to the tree, is finally captured
